feedback: If a learner says food travels through tubes straight to the leg muscle, point to the small-intestine wall: nutrients are absorbed INTO the blood there; the blood, not the gut, delivers them to cells.
If a learner places absorption in the stomach, clarify that most absorption happens in the small intestine (its folded, villi-covered surface is huge); the stomach mainly digests.
If a learner treats the two systems as unconnected, highlight the handover point at the intestine wall: digestion prepares soluble nutrients, circulation distributes them.
If a learner thinks blood only carries oxygen, remind them nutrients and water are also cargo, and waste is the return load.
activities.intendedInsight: The digestive and circulatory systems the child learned separately are one connected delivery network: the food you eat is absorbed into the blood and travels to every cell in your body.
learnerActions: Pick a mouthful of food and trace what happens to it as it is digested along the gut.
At the small-intestine wall, identify the pivotal moment: the nutrient crosses OUT of the gut tube and INTO a blood vessel (absorption).
Follow the nutrient as the heart pumps blood carrying it through the vessels out to a working muscle cell (e.g. a leg muscle) that grabs and uses it.
Note the co-passengers — water and oxygen riding along in the blood too — and the waste picked up for the return trip, so blood is understood as two-way transport.
Name each hand-off aloud or in writing: digested in the gut → absorbed into blood at the small intestine → carried by the circulatory system → delivered to the cell.
activities.title: Follow one nutrient from a meal to a working cell

feedback: If the traced line skips from gut straight to muscle, ask where the nutrient entered the blood — the path must cross the small-intestine wall into a vessel first.
If no return path is drawn, prompt: what happens to the waste the cell produces? Blood carries it away too.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing and narrating the whole path on a body makes the delivery network a route the learner can reconstruct and explain, not just recognise.
learnerActions: On a body outline, draw a meal in the gut and a target muscle (e.g. in the leg or toes).
Use a finger or a drawn/coloured line to trace the path from the drawn meal, through the gut, across the small-intestine wall into a blood vessel, through the pumping heart, and out to the muscle.
Narrate each hand-off between systems as you go ('here it's absorbed into the blood', 'here the heart pumps it on', 'here the cell uses it').
Add arrows showing waste returning from the cell back into the blood to show two-way transport.
activities.title: Trace the journey on a body outline

feedback: A complete explanation says: digested nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood; the circulatory system then carries the dissolved nutrients to every cell, including the leg muscle. The gut absorbs, the blood transports — they work together.
If the learner describes food reaching the leg through pipes with no absorption into blood, reteach the hand-off at the small intestine explicitly.
If the learner is vague about where absorption happens, point to the small intestine and its villi/surface area; the stomach mainly digests.

A vague answer that knows blood carries nutrients but cannot say where absorption happens or how the systems connect needs the absorption hand-off made explicit before it counts as a full explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands transport routes nutrients via absorption into the blood; one without it imagines food travelling bodily through the gut to its destination, with no role for blood.
learnerActions: Consider: after you digest your dinner, nutrients need to reach a muscle in your leg. A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and straight into the leg.
Explain how the nutrients actually get from gut to leg muscle: what carries them, and where do they cross over?

Answer the probing follow-ups: At which organ do nutrients pass out of the gut into the blood? Why does it help that the small intestine has a huge, folded inner surface? If the circulatory system stopped, why would a leg muscle starve even though there's food in the gut? How do the digestive and circulatory systems depend on each other to nourish a cell?
activities.title: Explain the diagnostic 'how do nutrients reach a leg muscle?' question
